sections.h2: Can a squatter take an Idaho house?
sections.html:
Only by meeting every element of the adverse possession statutes for a full 20 years, which is a hard test in Idaho. A short stay, a few months in a vacant house, or an occupant who moved in with no claim of right is nowhere close.

Idaho has two routes. One covers a person who claims title under a written instrument or a court judgment, and the other covers a person with no paper at all. Both require continuous occupation and possession for 20 years, and the second route adds proof that the land was enclosed or cultivated (Idaho Code 5-207 and 5-210).

For an owner the practical reading is simple. Someone who walks into your house and stays is a problem to solve quickly with the removal tools below, not a title risk that is ticking in any meaningful way.

sections.h2: What a claimant must prove to win by adverse possession
sections.html:
A claimant with no written instrument must show the land was protected by a substantial enclosure or usually cultivated or improved, and must prove it by clear and convincing evidence (Idaho Code 5-210). In no case is adverse possession established unless the land was occupied and claimed continuously for 20 years and the claimant, or the predecessors and grantors, paid all state, county and municipal taxes levied and assessed on it.

The tax element is a major hurdle. An owner who pays the property tax every year and keeps the receipts has a strong answer to a claim. A claimant who never paid the tax cannot meet the statute.

A claimant with a written instrument or judgment has a longer list of ways to show possession. Under Idaho Code 5-208, land counts as possessed in these cases:

  • It has been usually cultivated or improved.
  • It has been protected by a substantial enclosure.
  • Although not enclosed, it has been used for fuel, fencing timber, pasturage or the occupant's ordinary use.
  • A known farm or single lot has been partly improved, and the uncleared part follows the usual custom of the area.

The same clear and convincing standard applies to this route.

An owner can defeat a boundary or occupancy claim by recording a written instrument with the county recorder stating that the owner did not intend to define boundaries or ownership by permitting the possession. Both 5-208 and 5-210 contain this rule.

It helps most with neighbors and on rural land. If a neighbor's fence, driveway or garden crosses your line, a recorded statement can protect you without a lawsuit and without a fight. Record it in the real estate records of the county where the property sits, and expect the fee schedule in Idaho Code 31-3205 to apply.

If you plan to sell, a clean boundary helps. A buyer's title company will look at fences, shared drives and old agreements, and a recorded permission notice answers a question before anyone asks it.

sections.h2: Which Idaho law fits which kind of unwanted occupant?
sections.html:
The right tool depends on who is in the house and how they got there. Idaho has separate laws for tenants who stay, strangers who enter, and people who remain after being told to leave.

SituationIdaho lawWhat it does
Tenant stays past the lease or fails to payIdaho Code 6-303Unlawful detainer, the civil route to restitution after written notice
Stranger in a residence, owner wants them out nowIdaho Code 6-310AOwner asks the county sheriff for immediate removal on a verified complaint
Person refuses to leave or returns after noticeIdaho Code 18-7008Criminal trespass
Person claims title after many yearsIdaho Code 5-207, 5-208, 5-210Adverse possession, 20 years and tax payment

People who rent or once rented from you fall in a different category. The sheriff process described next does not cover them.

Idaho now lets an owner or the owner's authorized agent ask the county sheriff for immediate removal of people unlawfully occupying a residential dwelling. The law is Idaho Code 6-310A, created by House Bill 321 in 2025.

The owner has to meet every condition:

  • The requester is the owner or the owner's authorized agent.
  • The property includes a residential dwelling.
  • Unauthorized people entered unlawfully and remain or live there.
  • The property was not open to the public when they entered.
  • The owner has directed them to leave.
  • They are not current or former tenants under a written or oral rental agreement the owner authorized.
  • They are not immediate family members of the owner.
  • No litigation over the property is pending between the owner and any known occupant.

The owner submits a completed and verified "Complaint to Remove Persons Unlawfully Occupying Residential Real Property" to the sheriff of the county where the property is located. The sheriff is entitled to the same fee as for serving a writ of restitution. The statute was amended in 2026, so call the sheriff for the current text and the county form before you file.

sections.h2: When the occupant is or was a tenant
sections.html:
A former or current tenant has to be removed through unlawful detainer, not the sheriff shortcut. Under Idaho Code 6-303, a tenant who stays after the term ends without the landlord's permission commits unlawful detainer, and so does one who stays after a default in rent and a three day written notice that demands payment or possession.

The notice must also tell the tenant that, if a court enters judgment, a residential tenant has 72 hours, and a commercial tenant or one with a tract of five acres or more has seven days, to remove belongings before the landlord may dispose of them under section 6-316. Notice for a breach other than rent also runs three days, and the tenant has that time to cure the breach.

An agricultural tenant who holds over more than 60 days after the term ends, with no demand to leave or notice to quit from the landlord, is deemed to hold by permission and may stay another full year. Owners of farm or ranch land should read that rule closely before assuming a holdover can be removed quickly.

sections.h2: Criminal trespass for a house owner
sections.html:
A person commits criminal trespass by entering or remaining on another's real property without permission, knowing or having reason to know that presence is not permitted (Idaho Code 18-7008). Outside a landlord and tenant relationship, a person has reason to know when they fail to leave immediately after the owner or agent tells them to, or when they return without permission within one year.

The statute also finds reason to know on property reasonably associated with a residence or place of business, and on property fenced or enclosed so a reasonable person would see a private boundary. Penalties scale with the facts, with different tiers for first and repeat offenses. A related law, Idaho Code 18-3502, deals with unlawful re-entry of land after a person has been removed by process of law.

Keep your own records: a dated written instruction to leave, photographs, and a log of any return. They make it easier to show what you told the person and when.

sections.h2: Selling a house with an unwanted occupant
sections.html:
A house with a squatter can still be sold, but the occupant usually has to be gone, or the sale terms have to deal with it openly. An unresolved occupant can complicate a conventional sale, since a buyer or title company may ask for vacant possession or a clear lease.

Sellers who need to move faster can start with these steps:

  • Give written notice to leave and keep a copy.
  • Decide which route applies: sheriff removal, unlawful detainer or a trespass report.
  • Pay the property tax and keep receipts, which also defeat an adverse possession claim.
  • Tell any buyer about the occupant in writing.
  • Ask an Idaho attorney before you change locks, move belongings or cut off utilities.

A cash buyer may be willing to take on an occupied property as is, but that is a decision for each buyer and each house, and no result should be assumed in advance.

faqs.q: How long does it take to claim adverse possession in Idaho?
faqs.a: Twenty years of continuous occupation and possession under both the written instrument route and the no instrument route, and the claimant must also have paid all state, county and municipal taxes on the land.

faqs.q: Can I ask the sheriff to remove a squatter in Idaho?
faqs.a: Yes, if you meet every condition in Idaho Code 6-310A: the occupants entered unlawfully, you told them to leave, they are not current or former tenants or immediate family, and no litigation is pending. You file a verified complaint with the sheriff of the county where the home sits.

faqs.q: Is a former tenant a squatter under Idaho law?
faqs.a: No. A tenant who stays after the lease ends or after a rent default and notice is handled through unlawful detainer under Idaho Code 6-303, and the sheriff removal law excludes current and former tenants.

faqs.q: How much notice must a landlord give for unpaid rent in Idaho?
faqs.a: Three days written notice that states the amount due and demands payment or possession, under Idaho Code 6-303(2).

faqs.q: Does paying property tax protect me from a squatter's claim?
faqs.a: It helps a great deal. Idaho Code 5-210 requires a claimant to have paid all taxes levied and assessed on the land, so an owner who pays on time and keeps receipts leaves the claimant unable to satisfy that element.
